summary: Specifies protocol extensions for Diffserv-aware MPLS Traffic Engineering, which lets bandwidth be reserved separately per class of traffic. It generalizes existing routing-protocol extensions from RFC 3630 and RFC 3784, adds some new ones, and extends RSVP-TE signaling. This is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Ordinary MPLS traffic engineering treats all traffic as one bucket, so a flood of data can use up the space reserved for voice calls. RFC 4124 lets an operator set aside separate bandwidth pools for different kinds of traffic, and adds the signalling needed for routers to agree on which pool a new path belongs to.

questions: what is diffserv-aware mpls traffic engineering
what is a te-class in mpls
what is the classtype object in rsvp-te
subtitle: How MPLS traffic engineering learns to reserve bandwidth separately for each class of traffic, such as voice and data.

tldr.problem: Existing MPLS traffic engineering reserves bandwidth as one pool, so a provider cannot enforce different bandwidth limits for different classes of traffic, such as voice and data.
tldr.mechanism: Traffic is grouped into up to 8 Class-Types, each with its own bandwidth constraints. Pairs of Class-Type and preemption priority form TE-Classes, which the IGP advertises and RSVP-TE signals with a new CLASSTYPE object.
tldr.outcome: Routers can place each LSP using the bandwidth left for its own class, and ordinary MPLS TE is just the special case with one Class-Type.

today: RFC 4124 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2005, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It extends the traffic engineering additions to OSPF, IS-IS and RSVP that earlier RFCs defined.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The requirements document presents the service provider requirements for support of Diffserv-aware MPLS traffic engineering, which includes the fundamental requirement to be able to enforce different bandwidth constraints for different classes of traffic.

This document specifies the interior gateway protocol and RSVP-TE signalling extensions, beyond those already specified for existing MPLS traffic engineering, that support those requirements, including environments relying on distributed constraint-based routing, for example path computation involving head-end label switching routers.

The requirements document provides a definition and examples of bandwidth constraints models. This document does not specify or assume a particular model; specific models are outside its scope. Although the extensions here may not be sufficient to support all conceivable models, they do support the Russian Dolls Model, the Maximum Allocation Model and the Maximum Allocation with Reservation Model.

There may be differences between the quality of service expressed and obtained with Diffserv without DS-TE and with DS-TE. Because DS-TE uses constraint-based routing, and because of the type of admission control capabilities it adds to Diffserv, DS-TE has capabilities that Diffserv does not. Diffserv does not indicate preemption, by intent, whereas DS-TE describes multiple levels of preemption for its Class-Types. Diffserv also does not support any means of explicitly controlling overbooking, while DS-TE allows this.
sections.plainLanguage: The gap this fills is that plain Diffserv tells routers how to treat traffic once it arrives, but says nothing about reserving room for it. DS-TE adds that reservation, separately for each kind of traffic.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.content:
A traffic trunk is an aggregation of traffic flows of the same class, that is, treated equivalently from the DS-TE perspective, which is placed inside a label switched path.

A Class-Type is the set of traffic trunks crossing a link that is governed by a specific set of bandwidth constraints. A Class-Type is used for the purposes of link bandwidth allocation, constraint-based routing and admission control, and a given traffic trunk belongs to the same Class-Type on all links.

A TE-Class is a pair of a Class-Type and a preemption priority allowed for that Class-Type. This means that a label switched path transporting a traffic trunk from that Class-Type can use that preemption priority as the setup priority, the holding priority, or both.
sections.plainLanguage: Three terms carry the whole idea. A traffic trunk is a group of similar flows. A Class-Type is a pool of trunks that shares one bandwidth budget. A TE-Class is a Class-Type paired with the priority that traffic in it may use.

sections.title: Bandwidth Constraints on a Link
sections.content:
Regardless of the bandwidth constraints model, the solution must allow support for up to eight bandwidth constraints. For DS-TE the existing Maximum Reservable link bandwidth parameter is retained, but its semantics are generalised and interpreted as the aggregate bandwidth constraint across all Class-Types, so that, independently of the model in use, the sum of the bandwidth reserved for each Class-Type must not exceed the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth.

On every link, an implementation must provide for the configuration of up to eight additional link parameters, the eight potential bandwidth constraints, BC0 through BC7. The router must interpret these in accordance with the supported model, that is, what constraint applies to what Class-Type and how. Where the model imposes a relationship among the values, the router must enforce it at configuration time. With the Russian Dolls Model, for example, the router must ensure that BCi is configured smaller than or equal to BCj where i is greater than j, and that BC0 equals the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth. With the Maximum Allocation Model, it must ensure that all BCi are configured smaller than or equal to the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth.

DS-TE also lets an administrator apply different overbooking ratios for different Class-Types. The two principal methods are the same as those historically used in traffic engineering deployments: taking the ratio into account for the ordered aggregate or Class-Type associated with the path when establishing the bandwidth size of a given path, which the RFC calls LSP size overbooking, and taking the ratio into account when configuring the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth and the constraints, which it calls link size overbooking.
sections.plainLanguage: Each link keeps the usual total bandwidth number, plus up to eight smaller numbers, one per class. How those smaller numbers relate to each other depends on the model the operator has chosen.

sections.title: The TE-Class Mapping
sections.content:
The preemption attributes defined in the traffic engineering requirements are retained with DS-TE and apply within and across all Class-Types. The semantics of setup priority and holding priority are unchanged and are not affected by the Class-Type of a path. If one path contends with another for resources, it may preempt the other if it has a higher setup preemption priority, meaning a lower numerical priority value, regardless of their Class-Types.

A DS-TE router must allow configuration of a TE-Class mapping in which the Class-Type and preemption level are configured for each of up to eight TE-Classes, written as TE-Class[i] paired with a Class-Type c and a preemption priority p, where 0 is at most i, c and p up to 7. Two TE-Classes must not be identical, meaning they must not have both the same Class-Type and the same preemption priority.

There are no other restrictions on how the Class-Types can be paired with the preemption priorities. One preemption priority can be paired with two or more Class-Types, and one Class-Type can be paired with two or more preemption priorities. Where the administrator uses fewer than eight TE-Classes, the rest may be configured as unused, and configuring all eight as unused effectively disables the traffic engineering. To ensure coherent operation, the administrator must configure exactly the same TE-Class mapping on all routers of the DS-TE domain. When the mapping needs to be modified, care should be taken during the transient period, and it is recommended that active tunnels do not use any of the TE-Classes being modified.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator builds a table with eight rows. Each row says which class of traffic may use which priority level. Every router in the network has to have the same table, or they will disagree about what a path is allowed to do.

sections.title: Advertising Bandwidth Constraints in the IGP
sections.content:
Up to eight bandwidth constraints are configurable on any given link. With DS-TE the existing Maximum Reservable Bandwidth sub-TLV is retained with generalised semantics, so that it must now be interpreted as the aggregate bandwidth constraint across all Class-Types, independently of the model in use.

The document also defines a new optional sub-TLV to advertise the eight potential constraints. It carries a Bandwidth Constraints Model Id of one octet, a Reserved field of three octets, and the constraints themselves, each encoded on 32 bits in IEEE floating point format. The units are bytes per second, not bits. With OSPF the sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the Link TLV and its type is 17; with IS-IS it is a sub-TLV of the extended IS reachability TLV and its type is 22. The reserved field should be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

Where the configured TE-Class mapping and the model in use make the later constraints irrelevant to any configured Class-Type, it is recommended that only the constraints from BC0 up to the last relevant one are advertised, in order to minimise the impact on IGP scalability.

A router may optionally advertise the constraints, but if it does it must use the new sub-TLV in addition to the existing Maximum Reservable Bandwidth sub-TLV. A router receiving the sub-TLV with a model identifier that does not match the model it uses should warn the operator about the inconsistency. If it does not support the model named, or does not support operations with multiple simultaneous models, it may discard the TLV; if it does support them, it may accept it and allow different models to be used in different parts of the domain.

The existing Unreserved Bandwidth sub-TLV is retained as the only vehicle for advertising the dynamic bandwidth information needed for constraint-based routing, with generalised semantics. It still carries eight bandwidth values, but they now correspond to the unreserved bandwidth for each of the TE-Classes rather than for each preemption priority, and they are arranged in increasing order of TE-Class index. The values are in IEEE floating point format and the units are bytes per second. Because the values are now ordered by TE-Class index, a router must not assume any ordered relationship among them.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocol has to carry the extra numbers so that other routers can compute a path. Two new pieces are added: a list of the class budgets, and a rework of the existing free-bandwidth list so that it has one entry per class rather than one per priority.

sections.title: The CLASSTYPE Object
sections.content:
One new RSVP object is defined: the CLASSTYPE object, which is applicable to Path messages and is used only for establishing tunnels that contain a session object with a Class-Type of LSP_TUNNEL_IPv4 and a LABEL_REQUEST object. It is optional with respect to RSVP so that general RSVP implementations not concerned with MPLS tunnel setup do not have to support it, but a router supporting DS-TE must support it.

The object has a Class Number of 66 and one defined C-Type, which is 1. Its body is a 29-bit Reserved field, which must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and a 3-bit CT field giving the Class-Type. The values currently allowed are 1 through 7; the value 0 is reserved.

To establish a tunnel, the sender creates a Path message with a session type of LSP_Tunnel_IPv4 and a LABEL_REQUEST object, and may also include the DIFFSERV object. If the path is associated with Class-Type 0 the sender must not include the CLASSTYPE object, which allows backward compatibility with routers that are not DS-TE capable. If the path is associated with Class-Type N, where N is 1 to 7, the sender must include the object with the CT field set to N. If a Path message contains multiple CLASSTYPE objects, only the first is meaningful and the rest must be ignored and not forwarded. Each router along the path must record the object in its path state block, and if it is absent the router must associate Class-Type 0 with the path. The destination router must not include a CLASSTYPE object in its Resv message.

A router that recognises the object must send a PathErr with the error code Diffserv-aware TE Error in several situations: when the object appears in a message that has no LABEL_REQUEST or no LSP_Tunnel_IPv4 session type, with the error value Unexpected CLASSTYPE object; when it does not support the particular Class-Type, with the value Unsupported Class-Type; when the Class-Type value is not valid, with the value Invalid Class-Type value; and when the Class-Type paired with the setup priority or the holding priority does not form one of the configured TE-Classes, with the matching error values. A router that does not recognise the class number must behave as for an unknown Class-Num and send a PathErr with the error code Unknown object class.
sections.plainLanguage: The path message gains one small field saying which class the path belongs to. Class 0 is left out of the message entirely, so old routers keep working.

sections.title: Existing TE as a Particular Case
sections.content:
Existing traffic engineering can be viewed as a particular case of DS-TE in which a single Class-Type is used, all eight preemption priorities are allowed for that Class-Type, and the TE-Class mapping pairs TE-Class[i] with Class-Type 0 and preemption priority i, for 0 at most i up to 7. In that case DS-TE behaves as existing TE.

As with existing TE, the routing protocol advertises unreserved bandwidth for each of the eight preemption priorities, and may advertise a Maximum Reservable Bandwidth containing a constraint that applies across all paths. Because all paths transport traffic from Class-Type 0, the signalling is done without explicit signalling of the Class-Type, exactly as in existing TE.

The document also notes that details of admission control algorithms are left for vendor differentiation, but the advertised values must be consistent with the local algorithm and must take into account the holding preemption priority of established paths. Regardless of how the local algorithm computes the unreserved bandwidth, a path of bandwidth B, setup preemption priority p and Class-Type CTc is admissible on a link if and only if B is at most the unreserved bandwidth for the TE-Class that maps to CTc and p in the locally configured mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: If an operator only ever uses one class of traffic, the whole mechanism collapses back into the older behaviour, which is why this can be deployed without changing anything on the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not introduce additional security threats beyond those described for Diffserv and for MPLS traffic engineering, and the same security measures and procedures described in those documents apply here. For example, the approach for defence against theft and denial-of-service attacks discussed in the Diffserv architecture, which consists of the combination of traffic conditioning at the boundary nodes of a Diffserv domain with security and integrity of the network infrastructure within it, may be followed when DS-TE is in use.

It is specifically important that manipulation of administratively configurable parameters, such as those related to DS-TE paths, be executed in a secure manner by authorised entities.
sections.plainLanguage: No new security risk is claimed here. The one thing the RFC underlines is that changing the class and priority configuration is a privileged action and should be protected.

viz.caption: THE THREE TERMS THAT CARRY THE IDEA

items.title: Traffic trunk
items.text: A group of traffic flows of the same class, carried inside a label switched path.

items.title: Class-Type
items.text: The set of traffic trunks crossing a link that share one set of bandwidth constraints. The same trunk has the same Class-Type on every link.

items.title: TE-Class
items.text: A Class-Type paired with a preemption priority. An LSP may use that priority as its setup priority, its holding priority, or both.

items.title: Bandwidth constraint
items.text: A per-link budget of bandwidth for one Class-Type. Up to eight can be configured on a link, as BC0 through BC7.

viz.caption: THE BANDWIDTH CONSTRAINTS SUB-TLV AS DRAWN IN RFC 4124

fields.name: Bandwidth Constraints Model Id
fields.desc: A 1-octet identifier for the bandwidth constraints model in use by the router sending the advertisement.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Should be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: BC0 value
fields.desc: One bandwidth constraint, in IEEE floating point format, in bytes per second. Further values follow for BC1 onwards.

viz.caption: THE CLASSTYPE OBJECT AS DRAWN IN RFC 4124

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be set to zero on transmission and must be ignored on receipt.

fields.name: CT
fields.desc: The Class-Type. Values 1 to 7 are allowed and 0 is reserved.

viz.caption: THE Diffserv-AWARE TE ERROR AND ITS ERROR VALUES

items.label: DIFFSERV-AWARE TE ERROR
items.desc: The RSVP error code under which the values below are reported.

items.label: UNEXPECTED CLASSTYPE OBJECT
items.desc: The object appeared where a tunnel could not be set up.

items.label: UNSUPPORTED CLASS-TYPE
items.desc: The router does not support the Class-Type that was signalled.

items.label: INVALID CLASS-TYPE VALUE
items.desc: The signalled Class-Type value was not valid.

items.label: CT AND SETUP PRIORITY DO NOT FORM A CONFIGURED TE-CLASS
items.desc: The pair sent in the message is not in the router's TE-Class mapping.

items.label: CT AND HOLDING PRIORITY DO NOT FORM A CONFIGURED TE-CLASS
items.desc: The pair sent in the message is not in the router's TE-Class mapping.

items.label: BOTH PRIORITIES FAIL
items.desc: Neither the setup nor the holding priority forms a configured TE-Class with the Class-Type.

items.label: INCONSISTENCY BETWEEN SIGNALED PSC AND CT
items.desc: The scheduling class in the DIFFSERV object contradicts the Class-Type.

items.label: INCONSISTENCY BETWEEN SIGNALED PHBs AND CT
items.desc: The per-hop behaviours in the DIFFSERV object contradict the Class-Type.
